related_questions.question: How do you treat hand foot and mouth disease?

text_blocks.snippet: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is typically a mild, self-limiting viral illness. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications. There is no specific antiviral medication for HFMD.
snippet_highlighted_words: Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of treatment and care:

list.title: Fever and Pain:
list.snippet: Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) can help manage fever and discomfort.

list.title: Mouth Sores:
list.snippet: Topical oral anesthetics (available over the counter) can help relieve pain from mouth sores, making it easier to eat and drink.

list.title: Hydration:
list.snippet: Ensure the child drinks plenty of fluids, as dehydration can be a concern, especially if mouth sores make it painful to swallow. Popsicles can be a soothing option for sore throats.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: Offer soft, bland foods that are easy to swallow if the child is experiencing mouth pain.

list.title: Severe Pain:
list.snippet: If the child is experiencing severe pain or discomfort despite pain relievers, consult a healthcare provider.

list.title: Dehydration:
list.snippet: Signs of dehydration, such as decreased urination, dry skin, or lethargy, warrant medical attention.

list.title: Worsening Symptoms:
list.snippet: If symptoms worsen after a few days or if there are signs of secondary infection (like pus or increased redness around blisters), seek medical advice.

list.title: Infants under Six Months:
list.snippet: Consult a healthcare provider if your child is younger than six months, as they may be more susceptible to complications.

list.title: Weakened Immune System:
list.snippet: If the child has a weakened immune system, it's crucial to seek medical advice promptly.

list.title: Hygiene:
list.snippet: Frequent and thorough handwashing, especially after contact with the infected person or their belongings, is crucial.

list.title: Disinfection:
list.snippet: Clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and shared items like toys.

list.title: Isolation:
list.snippet: Keep infected children away from others, especially during the first week of illness, and until fever and mouth sores have resolved.

list.title: Avoid Close Contact:
list.snippet: Avoid close contact, such as hugging or kissing, with infected individuals.
Most children can return to school or daycare after the fever has subsided and mouth sores have started to heal (usually within a week).
Children with widespread blisters may need to stay home until the blisters have dried.
Antibiotics are not effective against HFMD as it's a viral illness.
HFMD is usually a mild illness, and most people recover fully within 7-10 days.

related_questions.question: How to prevent hand foot mouth from spreading?

text_blocks.snippet: To prevent the spread of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD), focus on hygiene and limiting exposure. Frequent and thorough handwashing, especially after using the toilet, changing diapers, and before eating, is crucial. Disinfecting surfaces like doorknobs and toys, and avoiding close contact with infected individuals, are also important preventative measures, according to the CDC.
snippet_highlighted_words: focus on hygiene and limiting exposure

list.title: Frequent Handwashing:
list.snippet: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, particularly after using the toilet, changing diapers, and before eating or handling food.

list.title: Disinfecting Surfaces:
list.snippet: Regularly clean and disinfect surfaces like doorknobs, tables, and toys, especially in areas where infected individuals have been.

list.title: Avoid Close Contact:
list.snippet: Minimize close contact with individuals who have HFMD, such as hugging, kissing, or sharing utensils.

list.title: Keep Hands Away from Face:
list.snippet: Avoid touching your face, especially your eyes, nose, and mouth, to prevent the virus from entering your body.

list.title: Stay Home When Sick:
list.snippet: If you or your child has HFMD, stay home from work or school until symptoms improve to prevent further transmission.

list.title: Proper Hygiene During Illness:
list.snippet: If HFMD is diagnosed, keep any blisters clean and covered, and seek medical advice if needed.

list.title: Limit Sharing:
list.snippet: Discourage children from sharing items like cups, utensils, and toys that could easily transmit the virus.

list.title: Educate Children:
list.snippet: Teach children about the importance of handwashing and avoiding contact with others who are sick.

list.title: Vaccination:
list.snippet: While there is no vaccine in the United States to protect against HFMD, maintaining good hygiene practices is the best defense.

text_blocks.snippet: By implementing these preventative measures, you can significantly reduce the risk of contracting and spreading hand, foot, and mouth disease, according to Jefferson Health.

related_questions.question: How long is hand foot mouth contagious?

text_blocks.snippet: Hand, foot, and mouth disease is contagious for about a week, particularly during the first few days when fever is present. However, the virus can remain in the body and continue to be contagious for several days, even after symptoms begin to improve. The virus can be spread through direct contact with blisters or bodily fluids, and even through stool for several weeks.

list.title: During the fever:
list.snippet: HFMD is most contagious during the first few days when a fever is present.

list.title: After the fever:
list.snippet: While the level of contagiousness decreases, the virus can still be spread through direct contact with blisters or bodily fluids.

list.title: Through stool:
list.snippet: The virus can remain in the stool for several weeks, even after other symptoms have subsided.

list.title: Overall:
list.snippet: The infectious period is generally considered to be from a few days before symptoms appear until about a week after they begin.

text_blocks.snippet: Good hygiene practices, such as frequent handwashing, are crucial for preventing the spread of the virus.

related_questions.question: Can you go to work with hand, foot, and mouth?

text_blocks.snippet: No, it's generally not recommended for adults to go to work with hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). HFMD is highly contagious, and while it's more common in children, adults can also get it. Staying home from work, especially during the first few days when symptoms are most active, helps prevent spreading the virus to colleagues.
snippet_highlighted_words: No, it's generally not recommended for adults to go to work with hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD)

text_blocks.snippet: Here's why and what to do:

list.title: Contagious nature:
list.snippet: HFMD spreads through close contact, respiratory droplets, and contact with contaminated surfaces.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Adults may experience fever, sore throat, and painful blisters on the hands, feet, and in the mouth.

list.title: Recommendation:
list.snippet: To prevent the spread, it's best to stay home until symptoms improve, especially if your job involves close contact with others.

list.title: When to return:
list.snippet: Ideally, you should be fever-free for at least 24 hours and any blisters should be scabbed over before returning to work.

list.title: Good hygiene:
list.snippet: Even after your symptoms improve, continue practicing good hygiene, such as frequent handwashing and disinfecting surfaces, to minimize the risk of transmission.

text_blocks.snippet: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a common viral illness, especially in young children, characterized by sores in the mouth and a rash on the hands and feet. It's typically mild and resolves on its own within 7 to 10 days.
snippet_highlighted_words: a common viral illness, especially in young children, characterized by sores in the mouth and a rash on the hands and feet

list.snippet: Fever: Often the first sign, lasting a few days.
Sore throat: Mouth sores can be painful and make eating and drinking uncomfortable.
Rash: Red spots or blisters on the palms of the hands, soles of the feet, and inside the mouth (cheeks, gums, and tongue). The rash may also appear on the arms, legs, and buttocks.
Other: Some individuals may experience a general feeling of being unwell, and some children might have loose stools.
HFMD is caused by viruses, most commonly Coxsackievirus A16, but other enteroviruses can also be responsible, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
The virus spreads through close contact with an infected person, including droplets from coughing or sneezing, or contact with contaminated surfaces or feces.
No specific antiviral treatment: Since it's a viral infection, antibiotics are not effective.
Symptom relief: Focus on making the child comfortable and hydrated.
Pain relievers: Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) can help manage pain and fever.
Hydration: Encourage plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration, especially if mouth sores are painful.
Soft foods: Offer soft foods that are easy to swallow, like yogurt, applesauce, or mashed potatoes.
Rest: Ensure adequate rest to aid recovery.
Stay home: Keep children out of school or daycare until they are feeling better and any blisters have dried.
Good hygiene: Frequent handwashing, especially after using the toilet or changing diapers, is crucial.
Avoid close contact: Limit contact with individuals who are sick.
Clean and disinfect: Regularly clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and toys.
